readings.c1s1:
¶
'''unsupported''' (un-su-pōr′ted), ''a.'' Not supported; not upheld; not sustained; not maintained; not countenanced; not aided.

'''unsupportedly''' (un-su-pōr′ted-li), ''adv.'' In an unsupported manner; without support.

'''unsuppressed''' (un-su-prest′), ''a.'' Not suppressed; not held or kept under; not subdued; not quelled; not put down: as, ''unsuppressed'' laughter or applause; ''unsuppressed'' rebellion.

'''unsure''' (un-shör′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unsure, unsewer;'' < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''sure.''] Not sure; not fixed; not certain. ''Shak.'', T. N., ii. 3. 50.

'''unsured''' (un-shörd′), ''a.'' Not made sure; not securely established.
{{smaller block|<poem>By this knot thou shalt so surely tie
Thy now ''unsured'' assurance to the crown.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, ii. 1. 471.}}}}

'''unsurely''' (un-shör′li), ''adv.'' In an unsure manner; unsafely; uncertainly. ''Daniel'', Civil Wars, ii.

'''unsurety†''' (un-shör′ti), ''n.'' Uncertainty; doubt. ''Sir T. More'', Works, p. 319.

'''unsurmountable''' (un-sėr-moun′tạ-bl), ''a.'' Insurmountable. ''Warburton'', Divine Legation, iv. § 2.

'''unsurpassable''' (un-sėr-pȧs′ạ-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being surpassed, excelled, or exceeded. ''Thackeray.''

'''unsurpassably''' (un-sėr-pȧs′ạ-bli), ''adv.'' In an unsurpassable manner or degree; so as not to be surpassed. ''Athenæum'', No. 3263, p. 599.

'''unsurpassed''' (un-sėr-pȧst′), ''a.'' Not surpassed, excelled, exceeded, or outdone. ''Byron'', Childe
readings.c1s2:
Harold, iv.

'''unsurrendered''' (un-su-ren′dėrd), ''a.'' Not surrendered; not given up or delivered: as, an ''unsurrendered'' prize. ''Cowper'', Iliad, vii.

'''unsusceptibility''' (un-su-sep-ti-bil′i̤-ti), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unsusceptible.

'''unsusceptible''' (un-su-sep′ti-bl), ''a.'' Not susceptible; insusceptible: as, ''unsusceptible'' of stain. ''Swift.''

'''unsuspect†''' (un-sus-pekt′), ''a.'' Unsuspected. ''Milton'', P. L., ix. 771.

'''unsuspected''' (un-sus-pek′ted), ''a.'' Not suspected. {{smaller|(''a'') Not considered as likely to have done an evil act or to have a disposition to evil: as, a person ''unsuspected'' of evil. ''Pope'', Moral Essays, iii., note. (''b'') Not imagined to exist; not surmised; not mistrusted: as, an ''unsuspected'' evil.}}

'''unsuspectedly''' (un-sus-pek′ted-li), ''adv.'' In an unsuspected manner; without suspicion. ''Milton'', Touching Hirelings.

'''unsuspectedness''' (un-sus-pek′ted-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unsuspected. ''Fuller'', Ch. Hist., X. ii. 27. (''Davies.'')

'''unsuspecting''' (un-sus-pek′ting), ''a.'' Not suspecting; unsuspicious; not imagining that any ill is designed.
{{smaller block|To circumvent an ''unsuspecting'' wight.
{{right|''Daniel'', Civil Wars, v.}}}}

'''unsuspectingly''' (un-sus-pek′ting-li), ''adv.'' In an unsuspecting manner; without suspicion.

'''unsuspectingness''' (un-sus-pek′ting-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unsuspecting; freedom from suspicion.
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''unswerving''' (un-swėr′ving), ''a.'' Not deviating from any rule, standard, or course; undeviating; unwavering; firm.

'''unswervingly''' (un-swėr′ving-li), ''adv.'' Without swerving; undeviatingly; firmly.

'''unsworn''' (un-swōrn′), ''a.'' Not sworn. {{smaller|(''a'') Not bound by an oath; not having taken an oath: as, an ''unsworn'' witness. (''b'') Not solemnly pronounced or taken.}}
{{smaller block|Her solemn oath remained ''unsworn.''
{{right|''Cowper'', Odyssey, x.}}}}

'''unsyllabled''' (un-sil′a̤-bld), ''a.'' Not syllabled; not articulated, uttered, or pronounced; not divided into syllables.

'''unsymmetric''' (un-si-met′rik), ''a.'' Same as ''unsymmetrical.''

'''unsymmetrical''' (un-si-met′ri-ka̤l), ''a.'' Lacking symmetry; asymmetrical: specifically, in botany, said of such flowers as lack numerical symmetry—that is, have the parts in the different cycles of unequal number. See ''symmetrical'', 5.

'''unsymmetrically''' (un-si-met′ri-ka̤l-i), ''adv.'' In an unsymmetrical manner; without symmetry.

'''unsymmetry''' (un-sim′e-tri), ''n.'' Want of symmetry; disproportion; asymmetry.
{{smaller block|Each member of a plant will display . . . ''unsymmetry'' or asymmetry where there is partial or entire departure from a balance of surrounding actions.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Biol. (Amer. ed. 1872), § 220.}}}}

'''unsympathizability''' (un-sim″pa̤-thī-za̤-bil′i-ti), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unsympa-

thizable.

'''unsympathizable''' (un-sim′pa̤-thī-za̤-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of awakening sympathy.

'''unsympathy''' (un-sim′pa̤-thi), ''n.'' Lack of sympathy.

'''unsupportedly''' (un-su-pōr′ted-li), ''adv.'' In an unsupported manner; without support.

'''unsuppressed''' (un-su-prest′), ''a.'' Not suppressed; not held or kept under; not subdued; not quelled; not put down: as, ''unsuppressed'' laughter or applause; ''unsuppressed'' rebellion.

'''unsure''' (un-shör′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unsure, unsewer;'' < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''sure.''] Not sure; not fixed; not certain. ''Shak.'', T. N., ii. 3. 50.

'''unsured''' (un-shörd′), ''a.'' Not made sure; not securely established.
{{smaller block|<poem>By this knot thou shalt so surely tie
Thy now ''unsured'' assurance to the crown.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, ii. 1. 471.}}}}

'''unsurely''' (un-shör′li), ''adv.'' In an unsure manner; unsafely; uncertainly. ''Daniel'', Civil Wars, ii.

'''unsurety†''' (un-shör′ti), ''n.'' Uncertainty; doubt. ''Sir T. More'', Works, p. 319.

'''unsurmountable''' (un-sėr-moun′tạ-bl), ''a.'' Insurmountable. ''Warburton'', Divine Legation, iv. § 2.

'''unsurpassable''' (un-sėr-pȧs′ạ-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being surpassed, excelled, or exceeded. ''Thackeray.''

'''unsurpassably''' (un-sėr-pȧs′ạ-bli), ''adv.'' In an unsurpassable manner or degree; so as not to be surpassed. ''Athenæum'', No. 3263, p. 599.

'''unsurpassed''' (un-sėr-pȧst′), ''a.'' Not surpassed, excelled, exceeded, or outdone. ''Byron'', Childe Harold, iv.

'''unsurrendered''' (un-su-ren′dėrd), ''a.'' Not surrendered; not given up or delivered: as, an ''unsurrendered'' prize. ''Cowper'', Iliad, vii.

'''unsusceptibility''' (un-su-sep-ti-bil′i̤-ti), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unsusceptible.

'''unsusceptible''' (un-su-sep′ti-bl), ''a.'' Not susceptible; insusceptible: as, ''unsusceptible'' of stain. ''Swift.''

'''unsuspect†''' (un-sus-pekt′), ''a.'' Unsuspected. ''Milton'', P. L., ix. 771.

'''unsuspected''' (un-sus-pek′ted), ''a.'' Not suspected. {{smaller|(''a'') Not considered as likely to have done an evil act or to have a disposition to evil: as, a person ''unsuspected'' of evil. ''Pope'', Moral Essays, iii., note. (''b'') Not imagined to exist; not surmised; not mistrusted: as, an ''unsuspected'' evil.}}

'''unsuspectedly''' (un-sus-pek′ted-li), ''adv.'' In an unsuspected manner; without suspicion. ''Milton'', Touching Hirelings.

'''unsuspectedness''' (un-sus-pek′ted-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unsuspected. ''Fuller'', Ch. Hist., X. ii. 27. (''Davies.'')

'''unsuspecting''' (un-sus-pek′ting), ''a.'' Not suspecting; unsuspicious; not imagining that any ill is designed.
{{smaller block|To circumvent an ''unsuspecting'' wight.
{{right|''Daniel'', Civil Wars, v.}}}}

'''unsuspectingly''' (un-sus-pek′ting-li), ''adv.'' In an unsuspecting manner; without suspicion.

'''unsuspectingness''' (un-sus-pek′ting-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unsuspecting; freedom from suspicion.

{{smaller block|Her quiet-eyed ''unsuspectingness'' only makes her the more a part of his delicate entertainment.
{{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Portraits of Places, p. 253.}}}}

'''unsuspicion''' (un-sus-pish′o̤n), ''n.'' Lack of suspicion; unsuspiciousness.
{{smaller block|Old men may come here, through their own heedlessness and ''unsuspicion.''
{{right|''Dickens.''}}}}

'''unsuspicious''' (un-sus-pish′us), ''a.'' Not suspicious. {{smaller|(''a'') Not inclined to suspect or imagine evil; unsuspecting.}}
{{smaller block|When a wagon-load of valuable merchandise had been smuggled ashore, at noonday, perhaps, and directly beneath their ''unsuspicious'' noses.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, p. 31.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Not raising, or tending to raise, suspicion: as, ''unsuspicious'' conduct. (''c'') Not passed in suspicion; free from anything likely to cause suspicion. [Rare.]}}
{{smaller block|But farewell now to ''unsuspicious'' nights.
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, iv. 565.}}}}

'''unsuspiciously''' (un-sus-pish′us-li), ''adv.'' In an unsuspicious manner; unsuspectingly; without suspicion.

'''unsuspiciousness''' (un-sus-pish′us-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unsuspicious.

'''unsustainable''' (un-sus-tā′na̤-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being sustained, maintained, or supported. ''Barrow'', Sermons, I. xviii.

'''unsustained''' (un-sus-tānd′), ''a.'' Not sustained; not maintained, upheld, or supported. ''Dryden'', Æneid, xi.

'''unswaddle''' (un-swod′l), ''v. t.'' To remove swaddling-bands from, as a young child; by extension, to unswathe; release from bandages, or the like.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Clay.'' Puppy has scarce ''unswaddled'' my legs yet.
''Turfe.'' What, wisps on your wedding-day?</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Tale of a Tub, i. 2.}}}}

'''unswathe''' (un-swāᴛ̵ʜ′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''swathe''<sup>1</sup>.] To take a swathe from; relieve from a bandage.
{{smaller block|In the morning an old woman came to ''unswathe'' me.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 90.}}}}

'''unswayable''' (un-swā′a̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''sway'' + ''-able''.] Incapable of being swayed, governed, or influenced by another. ''Shak.'', Cor., v. 6. 26.

'''unswayed''' (un-swād′), ''a.'' Not swayed. {{smaller|(''a'') Not wielded. ''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 4. 470. (''b'') Not biased, controlled, or influenced: as, ''unswayed'' by passion or ambition. ''Sandys'', Travailes (1652), p. 120.}}

'''unswayedness''' (un-swād′nes), ''n.'' The state of being unswayed; steadiness. ''Hales'', Remains, p. 246.

'''unswear''' (un-swãr′), ''v.'' '''I.''' ''trans.'' To recant, revoke, or recall by a subsequent oath; retract by a second oath; abjure.
{{smaller block|No more than he’ll ''unswear''. ''Shak.'', Othello, iv. 1. 31.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To recant or recall on oath.
{{smaller block|<poem>For who would not oft sweare,
And oft ''unsweare'', a Diademe to beare?</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Mother Hub. Tale.}}}}

'''unsweat†''' (un-swet′), ''v. t.'' To remove or reduce the sweating of; ease or cool after exercise or toil.
{{smaller block|The interim of ''unsweating'' themselves . . . may, with profit and delight, be taken up with solemn music.
{{right|''Milton'', On Education.}}}}

'''unsweating''' (un-swet′ing), ''a.'' Not sweating or perspiring: as, an ''unsweating'' brow. ''Dryden'', tr. of Juvenal, iii. 117.

'''unsweet''' (un-swēt′), ''a.'' [Formerly also in var. ''unsoot'', q. v.; < ME. ''unswete'', < AS. ''unswēte'', not sweet, < ''un-'', not, + ''swēte'', sweet: see ''un-''<sup>1</sup> and ''sweet''.] Not sweet, in any sense.
{{smaller block|<poem>Lete,
That is a flood of helle ''unswete''.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', House of Fame, l. 72.}}
With voice ''unsweet''. {{right|''J. Baillie.''}}}}

'''unsweeten''' (un-swē′tn), ''v. t.'' To deprive of sweetness; make unsweet.
{{smaller block|<poem>Were all my joys essential, and so mighty
As the affected world believes I taste,
This object were enough to ''unsweeten'' all.</poem>
{{right|''Chapman and Shirley'', Chabot, Admiral of France, v.}}}}

'''unswell†''' (un-swel′), ''v. i.'' [< ME. ''unswellen''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''swell''.] To cease from swelling.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ebben gan the welle
Of hire teres and the herte ''unswelle''.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 1146.}}}}

'''unswept''' (un-swept′), ''a.'' Not swept. {{smaller|(''a'') Not cleaned by passing or rubbing a brush, broom, or besom over. ''Shak.'', M. W. of W., v. 5. 48. (''b'') Not cleaned up or removed by sweeping, as dust. ''Shak.'', Cor., ii. 3. 126. (''c'') Not moved or passed over with a sweeping motion or action.}}
{{smaller block|Foam ''unswept'' by wandering gusts. {{right|''Cowper'', Iliad, xi.}}}}

'''unswerving''' (un-swėr′ving), ''a.'' Not deviating from any rule, standard, or course; undeviating; unwavering; firm.

'''unswervingly''' (un-swėr′ving-li), ''adv.'' Without swerving; undeviatingly; firmly.

'''unsworn''' (un-swōrn′), ''a.'' Not sworn. {{smaller|(''a'') Not bound by an oath; not having taken an oath: as, an ''unsworn'' witness. (''b'') Not solemnly pronounced or taken.}}
{{smaller block|Her solemn oath remained ''unsworn.''
{{right|''Cowper'', Odyssey, x.}}}}

'''unsyllabled''' (un-sil′a̤-bld), ''a.'' Not syllabled; not articulated, uttered, or pronounced; not divided into syllables.

'''unsymmetric''' (un-si-met′rik), ''a.'' Same as ''unsymmetrical.''

'''unsymmetrical''' (un-si-met′ri-ka̤l), ''a.'' Lacking symmetry; asymmetrical: specifically, in botany, said of such flowers as lack numerical symmetry—that is, have the parts in the different cycles of unequal number. See ''symmetrical'', 5.

'''unsymmetrically''' (un-si-met′ri-ka̤l-i), ''adv.'' In an unsymmetrical manner; without symmetry.

'''unsymmetry''' (un-sim′e-tri), ''n.'' Want of symmetry; disproportion; asymmetry.
{{smaller block|Each member of a plant will display . . . ''unsymmetry'' or asymmetry where there is partial or entire departure from a balance of surrounding actions.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Biol. (Amer. ed. 1872), § 220.}}}}

'''unsympathizability''' (un-sim″pa̤-thī-za̤-bil′i-ti), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unsympathizable.

'''unsympathizable''' (un-sim′pa̤-thī-za̤-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of awakening sympathy.

'''unsympathy''' (un-sim′pa̤-thi), ''n.'' Lack of sympathy. {{smaller block|How true the ''unsympathy'' as well as the sympathy of nature. ''Wilberforce'', in Life by R. G. Wilberforce, II. 305.
{{right|[(''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''unsystematic''' (un-sis-te-mat′ik), ''a.'' Not systematic; not founded upon or in accord with a system; not having a defined system or plan; lacking regular order, distribution, or arrangement.
{{smaller block|Desultory ''unsystematic'' endeavours.
{{right|''Burke'', On the Present Discontents (1771).}}}}
='''Syn.''' See ''irregular.''

'''unsystematical''' (un-sis-te-mat′i-ka̤l), ''a.'' Same as ''unsystematic.''

'''unsystematically''' (un-sis-te-mat′i-ka̤l-i), ''adv.'' In an unsystematic manner; irregularly.

'''untache†''', ''v. t.'' [ME., < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''tache''<sup>1</sup>.] To carve.
{{smaller block|''Vntache'' that curlewe. ''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 265.}}

'''untack''' (un-tak′), ''v. t.'' To separate (that which is tacked); disjoin; loosen; release.
{{smaller block|Sir, the little adoe which me thinks I find in ''untacking'' these pleasant Sophismes puts mee into the mood to tell you a tale ere I proceed further.
{{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., ii.}}}}

'''untackle''' (un-tak′l), ''v. t.'' [< late ME. ''untacklen''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''tackle.''] To unhitch; unharness.
{{smaller block|But vse to ''vntackle'' them once in a day.
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie, p. 62.}}}}

'''untainted<sup>1</sup>''' (un-tān′ted), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''tainted'', pp. of ''taint''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' Not rendered impure by admixture; not impregnated with foul matter: as, ''untainted'' air.
{{smaller block|Narcissus pining o’er the ''untainted'' stream.
{{right|''Keats'', To Leigh Hunt.}}}}
'''2.''' Not sullied; not stained; unblemished. {{smaller block|What stronger breastplate than a heart ''untainted?''
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 2. 232.}}}}
'''3.''' Not rendered unsavory by putrescence: as, ''untainted'' meat.

'''untainted<sup>2</sup>†''' (un-tān′ted), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''tainted'', pp. of ''taint''<sup>3</sup>, ''v.''] Not attainted; not charged with a crime; not accused.
{{smaller block|<poem>Within these five hours lived Lord Hastings,
''Untainted'', unexamined, free, at liberty.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iii. 6. 9.}}}}

'''untaintedly''' (un-tān′ted-li), ''adv.'' In an untainted manner; in a manner free from taint, stain, or blemish. ''South'', Sermons, V. i.

'''untaintedness''' (un-tān′ted-nes), ''n.'' The state of being untainted; freedom from taint, stain, or blemish. ''Bp. Hall'', Sermon on 1 John i. 5.

'''untaken''' (un-tā′kn), ''a.'' Not taken, in any sense.
{{smaller block|It cannot stand with the love and wisdom of God to leave such order ''untaken'' as is necessary for the due government of his Church. ''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, iii. 11.}}

'''untalented''' (un-tal′ẹn-ted), ''a.'' Not talented; not gifted; not accomplished or clever.
{{smaller block|This is the sort of stuff you must be satisfied with from a poor ''untalented'' girl.
{{right|''Richardson'', Sir Charles Grandison, vii. 6. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''untalked''' (un-tâkt′), ''a.'' Not talked or spoken. {{smaller|—'''Untalked of''', not talked or spoken about; not made the subject of talk. ''Shak.'', R. and J., iii. 2. 7.}}

'''untamable''' (un-tā′ma-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being tamed, domesticated, subjugated, or subdued; not to be rendered tame, docile, or serviceable to man; incapable of being brought from a wild, savage, barbarous, rude, or violent state: as, an ''untamable'' tiger; an ''untamable'' savage; ''untamable'' passions. ''Barrow'', Sermons, I. iii. Also ''untameable.''

'''untamableness''' (un-tā′mạ-bl-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being untamed. Also ''untameableness.''

'''untame''' (un-tām′), ''a.'' Not tame; wild.
{{smaller block|Ida, . . . nurse of beasts ''untame.''
{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, viii. 41.}}}}

'''untamed''' (un-tāmd′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''untamed, untemid, untemed;'' as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''tamed.''] Not tamed. {{smaller|(''a'') Not reclaimed from wildness; not domesticated; not made familiar with man: as, an ''untamed'' beast. ''Locke.''}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And her eye has a glance more sternly wild
Than even that of a forest child
In its fearless and ''untamed'' freedom should be.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', Mogg Megone.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Not subdued; not brought under control: as, a turbulent, ''untamed'' mind.}}
{{smaller block|A people very stubborn and ''untamed.''
{{right|''Spenser'', State of Ireland.}}}}

'''untamedness''' (un-tāmd′nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being untamed. ''Leighton'', Com. on 1 Peter v. (''Encyc. Dict.'')

'''untangibly''' (un-tan′ji-bli), ''adv.'' Intangibly.

'''untangle''' (un-tang′gl), ''v. t.'' To loose from tangles or intricacy; disentangle; hence, to free from embarrassment, doubt, or uncertainty; resolve; clear up; explain.
{{smaller block|''Untangle'' but this cruel chain. ''Prior'', False Friend, iii.}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
